catalog_quote: Accented vowels have a higher pitch (musical tone) than unaccented vowels, and appear near the end of the word. ... Accent is either final or non-final. Final accent falls on the last syllable (vowel) of the word and non-final accent falls on the second-last, third-last, or fourth-last syllable. ... In most cases, long vowels count as one unit for the odd/even count (5a). However, the long ⌊a:-⌋ indef prefix always counts as two (Figure 3.2), as do underlyingly (or usually) long vowels ... In a nutshell, even-numbered penults are always accented (and lengthened, if possible). In contrast, odd-numbered penults are only sometimes accented (and lengthened, if possible). More often than not, odd-numbered penults cannot be accented (or lengthened) and the third-last vowel is accented instead. ... sweep_summary: Cayuga (cayu1261) is in the catalog as weight-sensitive (even/odd parity + penult conditions), deciding source Dyck et al. 2024. Seven Glottolog title hits collapse to five works. Rueentan 2014 (MUN MA thesis) was open and is now with; its ch.1 §2.1 pp.7-8 restates the placement rule (final accent medially; utterance-finally the even-numbered penult, an odd-numbered penult only if open/non-laryngeal/non-a, else antepenult) and confirms the catalog's classification, but it is a secondary restatement (citing Foster 1982, Dyck 2009) and does not supersede Dyck et al. 2024. Not obtainable open: Hatcher Jr 2022 UB dissertation (no URL/DOI anywhere, ProQuest only; priority high, the only full instrumental+phonological study), Michelson 1983 Harvard dissertation = Michelson 1988 Kluwer book (Springer DOI 10.1007/978-94-009-2709-4 paywalled; HathiTrust 000926060 and archive.org comparativestudy0000mich both restricted; priority medium), Chafe 1977 in SCOPIL 4 (HathiTrust 007480182 search-only, OCLC 3795144; priority medium), Doherty 1993 Harvard dissertation (Harvard print/microfiche; acoustic correlates only; priority low). Second-hand characterisations of Michelson 1988, Chafe 1977 and Doherty 1993 from the on-disk Williams 2013 and Hancock-Teed 2021 theses all agree with the catalog's classification.org.

new_statements.quote: There are two separate accentual patterns: accent is final for words that are utterance-medial, as in (1a) below; accent is non-final when words are utterance-final or in isolation, as in (1b). ... Non-final accent placement refers to both edges of the word; it refers to the left edge through an even and odd syllable count, and to the right edge, with reference to the antepenult, penult, and final syllable (Foster 1982; Dyck 2009). When the penult is an even numbered syllable (counting from the left), it is always accented ... Odd-numbered penults are only accented if they are not closed and do not contain a laryngeal. If any conditions on odd-numbered penults apply, the antepenult is accented instead.
new_statements.citation: Rueentan, Behak. 2014. The prosody of Cayuga particles. MA thesis, Memorial University of Newfoundland. hdl 20.500.14783/12855
new_statements.reading: Pitch accent on nouns/verbs: final syllable utterance-medially; utterance-finally the penult if it is an even-numbered syllable from the left, or an odd-numbered penult only when it is open, laryngeal-free and not short [a]; otherwise the antepenult. This is the even/odd parity count plus weight/quality conditions the catalog codes as 'weight' from Dyck et al. 2024 §3.6; Rueentan adds that short words with a disqualified odd-numbered penult can surface unaccented (dagu:s, sekdǫ:, ǫˀnǫ:ˀ). One sentence in the passage is internally garbled (lists 'are closed' as a condition for accenting) but the following sentence and the examples fix the intended reading.

sources.note: Ch.1 §2.1 (pp.7-8) restates the noun/verb accent rule: final accent utterance-medially, non-final accent utterance-finally/in isolation; non-final accent counts even/odd syllables from the left and refers to antepenult/penult/final from the right; an even-numbered penult is always accented, an odd-numbered penult only when it lacks short [a], is open, and has no [h]/[ʔ] in the rhyme, otherwise the antepenult; short words can end up unaccented (dagu:s, sekdǫ:, ǫˀnǫ:ˀ). sources.quote: 'stress placement is driven by iterative, left-to-right, iambic footing with primary stress generally falling on the penult or antepenult on utterance final words and otherwise on the final syllable (Foster 1982; see also Chafe 1977, Dyck 1997, 2009, Michelson 1988). The phonetic correlate of primary stress is pitch accent (Doherty 1993; Williams 2013).' Also: 'Iambic footing is established iteratively from left to right... However, pitch accent placement is computed from the right edge (see Michelson 1988).'

sources.quote: 'Cayuga words have one metrically-prominent syllable that is realized with H tone... The accented syllable in Cayuga is either final or non-final. Final accent occurs in words which are utterance-medial. Non-final accent occurs in words that are isolated or at the end of a phrase' (pp.16-17). Appendix A tree: utterance-final word -> 'Counting from the left edge, is the second last vowel EVEN-numbered?' YES: accent it (penult); NO: is it an <a>? YES -> accent preceding vowel (antepenult); followed by a consonant cluster? YES -> antepenult; followed by t, k, j, h, or ʔ? YES -> antepenult; NO ->
